title: State v. Anmol
subcite: Ct. Case No. 189/2020 | CNR DLST01-002109-2020 | Special Court (Electricity), South District, Saket Courts, New Delhi
court: Special Court (Electricity), South District, Saket Courts, New Delhi
judge: Sh. Vivek Kumar Gulia, Addl. Sessions Judge
parties: State (BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.) v. Anmol (alleged user/owner) — the registered consumer (Narender Singh) having died
result: Acquitted — complaint dismissed. Meter tampering was confirmed by the laboratory, but the accused was not shown to be the user/owner — the grandfather named did not match, and suspicion cannot replace proof. The accused stands acquitted of the charge under Section 135 read with Sections 150 and 313 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
statutes: Section 135 (and third proviso to s. 135(1)), Electricity Act, 2003

interpretations.provision: Section 135(1) — Theft of Electricity: the Foundational Facts
interpretations.interpretation: The Court read Section 135(1) as requiring the prosecution first to prove, beyond reasonable doubt, the foundational facts — an unauthorised or artificial abstraction of electricity and the identity of the accused as its author or as the consumer/user of the inspected premises. Only upon proof of those facts does the offence, or the abetment of it, arise; a bare allegation, or mere presence at or near the spot, is not enough. As the Act does not define “dishonestly,” Section 24 IPC is imported, but dishonest intention presupposes an abstraction first fixed on the accused.

interpretations.provision: Third Proviso to Section 135(1) — When the Presumption Does Not Arise
interpretations.interpretation: The reverse-onus presumption of dishonest use operates only after the prosecution has established the artificial means of abstraction and connected it to the accused. Where that foundation fails — the inspection is self-contradictory, the user’s identity is not fixed, material witnesses are withheld, the electronic record is not duly certified under Section 65B, or the officer’s authority to complain is not proved — the presumption never arises. The ordinary rule then governs: the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and where two views are reasonably possible the one favouring the accused is adopted.

significance.point: Proof of tampering is not proof of the tamperer
significance.explanation: A confirmed lab finding fixes the act, not the person; identity must be independently proved.
Where the grandfather named does not match the accused, the link to the premises is broken.
However strong the suspicion of tampering, a conviction needs legal proof of the accused’s identity as user/owner.

significance.point: A deceased registered consumer sharpens the identity gap
significance.explanation: With the registered consumer dead, the prosecution had to prove the accused’s own status — and could not.

generic_facts.theft_mode: Meter tampering with magnetic device (remote control), broken seals, illegal PCB circuit connected inside meter
